targetLicense: ordinary non-commercial Class C passenger driver license

rules.authoringRule: A circular green signal lets a driver go straight or turn right or left unless a sign prohibits the turn, but the driver must yield to vehicles lawfully in the intersection and must stop and yield to pedestrians or sidewalk users lawfully in the intersection or an adjacent crosswalk. A green arrow permits a cautious entry only for the movement the arrow shows, with the same yielding duties.

A steady yellow signal warns that the movement allowed by the green is ending and that a red signal is about to appear. The driver should stop if it can be done safely rather than speed up to beat the change.

Facing a steady red signal, the driver must stop at the clearly marked stop line; with no stop line, before entering the near-side crosswalk. A vehicle that is not turning stays stopped until an indication to proceed appears. At a signal away from an intersection the stop is made at the marked stop point, or at the signal when nothing is marked.

After stopping at a steady red signal and waiting until the intersection can be entered safely, a driver may turn right, or turn left when both streets are one-way and the left turn is otherwise permissible. The driver must yield to pedestrians and traffic as after a stop sign, and a posted notice at the intersection can prohibit the turn on red.
conditions: yield to pedestrians and other traffic lawfully using the intersection
exceptions: posted notice prohibiting the turn on red

rules.authoringRule: A steady red arrow means stop for the movement it points to, at the stop line, the near-side crosswalk or the intersection edge, and remain stopped until an indication to proceed appears. Under the Texas MUTCD the same turn-on-red allowance applies to a red arrow as to a circular red: after stopping, a right turn, or a left turn from a one-way street into a one-way street, is permitted in the arrow direction unless a traffic control device prohibits turning on red, subject to stop-sign yielding rules.
conditions: movement limited to the arrow direction
yield as after a stop sign
exceptions: a NO TURN ON RED or similar device prohibits the turn
rules.reviewNote: Meaning taken from Texas MUTCD 2025 §4A.03 C.2, which Texas adopts by rule; Transportation Code §544.007 speaks only of a "steady red signal". Confirm the Texas Driver Handbook (DL-7, January 2026) teaches the same red-arrow allowance before production.

rules.authoringRule: A flashing yellow arrow allows a cautious turn in the arrow direction, but the turn is not protected: the driver must yield to pedestrians lawfully in the crosswalk and to other vehicles lawfully using the intersection, and a left turn must yield to oncoming traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard.

A flashing red signal requires a stop at the stop line, or before the near-side crosswalk, or at the point nearest the intersecting roadway with a view of approaching traffic; the driver then proceeds under the rules that apply after stopping at a stop sign. A flashing yellow signal allows the driver to proceed only with caution. These rules do not apply at a railroad crossing.

When a traffic signal shows no indication in any head, other than a freeway ramp meter or a pedestrian hybrid beacon, each driver must stop as if the intersection had a stop sign and yield before proceeding.

Overhead lane-use control signals govern one lane each: a steady downward green arrow means the lane is open in that direction, a steady yellow X warns that the lane is about to close and a red X will follow, and a steady red X means the lane is closed to traffic in that direction. White left-turn arrows mark a lane open only for left turns.

Where a pedestrian control signal shows WALK, DON'T WALK or WAIT, a pedestrian or sidewalk user may cross on WALK and every driver must stop and yield to them; nobody may start crossing on DON'T WALK or WAIT, but a person who started on WALK continues to a sidewalk or safety island while DON'T WALK or WAIT shows. Turning drivers keep yielding until that person has cleared their path.

At a stop sign, stop at the clearly marked stop line; if there is none, before entering the crosswalk on the near side; if there is no crosswalk, at the place nearest the intersecting roadway where approaching traffic can be seen, before entering the intersection.

At a yield sign the driver slows to a speed reasonable for the conditions, yields to vehicles in the intersection or approaching closely enough to be an immediate hazard, and stops when safety requires it, using the same stopping points as a stop sign.

After stopping at a stop sign or slowing at a yield sign, the driver must yield to vehicles that are in the intersection or approaching so closely on the other roadway that entering would be an immediate hazard, and may proceed only after that yielding. A driver who passes a yield sign without stopping and then collides with a vehicle in the intersection is treated as prima facie evidence of failing to yield.
A driver about to enter or cross a highway from an alley, building, private road or driveway must yield to vehicles approaching on the highway.

A driver coming out of an alley, building, private road or driveway in a business or residence district must stop before moving onto the sidewalk or the sidewalk area extending across the exit, yield to pedestrians and other traffic on the sidewalk, and then yield to vehicles on the roadway before entering it.

A driver may not stop, stand or park a vehicle in an intersection, on a crosswalk, or on a railroad track. Entering on a green light is therefore only lawful when the vehicle can clear the far side; otherwise wait behind the line so the intersection, crosswalk and tracks stay open.

A right turn is approached and completed as close as practicable to the right curb or edge. A left turn is approached from the extreme left lane lawfully available in the driver's direction and finished in a lane lawfully available to traffic in that direction on the road entered; on a two-way street the turn is made to the left of the intersection center. Official traffic control devices may require a different course.
A driver may not turn into a private road or driveway, turn from a direct course, or move right or left on a roadway unless the movement can be made safely.

A driver must signal an intention to turn, change lanes or start from a parked position, and must signal a right or left turn continuously for at least the last 100 feet before the turn. Turn signals may not be used as a courtesy or "do pass" message to a driver behind.

Signals may be given by signal lamps or by hand and arm from the left side of the vehicle: hand and arm extended horizontally means a left turn, extended upward means a right turn, and extended downward means a stop or a decrease of speed. A bicyclist may signal a right turn with the right hand and arm extended horizontally.

A driver turning left at an intersection, into an alley, or into a private road or driveway must yield to a vehicle approaching from the opposite direction that is in the intersection or close enough to be an immediate hazard.

A driver may not drive faster than is reasonable and prudent under the existing circumstances, must control speed to avoid colliding with anyone on or near the highway, and must slow when approaching and crossing an intersection or railroad crossing, on a curve or the crest of a hill, on a narrow or winding roadway, and whenever a special hazard exists because of traffic, weather or road conditions.

Unless a different limit is lawfully posted, these speeds are lawful when no special hazard requires less: 30 mph on an urban district street and 15 mph in an alley; 70 mph on a state- or U.S.-numbered highway outside an urban district, including farm-to-market and ranch-to-market roads; 60 mph on other highways outside an urban district; and 15 mph on a beach. Exceeding them is prima facie evidence that the speed is not reasonable and prudent.

The Texas Transportation Commission may set reasonable and safe posted limits after an engineering study; it may not set a limit above 75 mph in general, may post up to 80 mph on parts of Interstate 10 and Interstate 20 in named West Texas counties, and may post up to 85 mph on a highway designed to accommodate that speed. The posted number is the ceiling wherever it applies.

A driver may not drive so slowly as to impede the normal and reasonable movement of traffic unless a reduced speed is necessary for safe operation or to comply with the law. Posted minimum limits, where set, may not be driven under except for the same reasons.

A following driver must keep an assured clear distance behind the vehicle ahead, judged by the vehicles' speed, the traffic and the highway conditions, so that the driver can stop safely without hitting that vehicle or veering into another vehicle, object or person. Outside business and residential districts, vehicles in a caravan or motorcade, and trucks or vehicles towing that follow another such vehicle, must leave enough space for a passing vehicle to move in.

A time-based cushion is the practical way to keep the assured clear distance the law requires: count at least 2 seconds behind the vehicle ahead in good conditions and stretch it to 3 or 4 seconds when the road is wet, visibility is poor, or you are behind a large vehicle. The interval is guidance, not a statutory number.

rules.authoringRule: A driver must comply with every applicable official traffic-control device unless directed otherwise by a traffic officer, police officer or escort flagger. A device that is not in proper position or is not legible to an ordinarily observant person cannot be enforced, but rules that do not depend on a device apply regardless.

A person may not wilfully refuse a lawful order or direction of a police officer, of a school crossing guard performing crossing-guard duties or directing traffic in a school crossing zone, or of an escort flagger controlling traffic for a permitted oversize vehicle. Their direction overrides the normal signal or sign.

Texas classifies signs by function: regulatory signs give notice of traffic laws or regulations, warning signs give notice of a situation that might not be readily apparent, and guide signs show route designations, destinations, directions, distances, services and points of interest.

Distinctive shapes are reserved for specific messages: the octagon for STOP, the downward-pointing equilateral triangle for YIELD, the pennant for NO PASSING ZONE, the pentagon for school signs, the circle for the railroad advance warning, the diamond for warning signs, and the rectangle for most regulatory and guide signs.

Sign colors carry consistent meanings: red for stop, yield and prohibition; yellow for general warning; orange for temporary traffic control; fluorescent yellow-green for pedestrian, bicycle and school warnings; fluorescent pink for incident management; white for regulation; green for permitted movements and directional guidance; blue for road-user services; and brown for recreational and cultural interest guidance.

Intersection lane control signs tell drivers which movements are required or permitted from a specific lane; a sign mounted over a lane applies to that lane, and a supplemental plaque may limit a regulation to stated hours, days or vehicle types. The sign's words, symbols, plaque and lane position together give the actual instruction.

A DO NOT ENTER sign marks the entrance to a roadway or ramp that is closed to traffic in that direction, such as where a two-way road becomes one-way or at an exit ramp; a WRONG WAY sign farther in warns a driver who has already entered against traffic. The response is to avoid the entrance or, if already inside, to stop worsening the exposure and leave safely.

A yellow advisory speed plaque below a warning sign, or an advisory speed on a curve or ramp sign, recommends a safe speed for the condition ahead, such as a curve or exit ramp; it is guidance about the hazard, not a separate legal speed limit, and the posted regulatory limit remains the ceiling.

Warning signs are yellow diamonds whose symbols name the condition ahead: curves and turns, intersections, merges and added lanes, lane ends, divided highway begins or ends, two-way traffic, slippery when wet, signal ahead, stop ahead, and animal or pedestrian crossings. Their purpose is to give drivers time to slow or reposition before the hazard.

School area and school crossing signs use the pentagon shape in fluorescent yellow-green; a school speed limit sign with a WHEN FLASHING beacon or stated hours makes the lower limit regulatory during those times. Expect children, crossing guards and buses and widen the scan to sidewalks and crossings.

Guide signs use green for destinations, directions, distances and route markers, blue for motorist services such as fuel, food, lodging and hospitals, and brown for recreational and cultural sites. They support navigation and should be read early so lane changes happen without sudden moves.

Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions and mark the left edge of a divided or one-way roadway; white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction and mark the right edge. A broken line may be crossed when the maneuver is safe and otherwise lawful, a solid line discourages or prohibits crossing, and a double solid line prohibits crossing except where turning across it into a driveway is allowed.

values.yellow: separates opposing directions or marks the left edge of a divided or one-way roadway
values.white: separates same-direction lanes or marks the right edge

rules.authoringRule: A no-passing zone on a two-way road is marked by a solid yellow line on the side of traffic that may not pass; a double solid yellow center line means neither direction may pass, while a broken yellow line beside a solid one permits passing only from the broken-line side. The pennant-shaped NO PASSING ZONE sign marks the start of the zone.

A driver may not drive on the left side of the roadway in a no-passing zone or to the left of pavement striping that marks one; the state or a local authority marks the beginning and end of each zone with signs or markings. Crossing the striping, or the center line in a zone marked by signs only, to turn left into or out of an alley, private road or driveway is not prohibited.
exceptions: left turn into or out of an alley, private road or driveway

rules.authoringRule: A lane-use arrow painted in a lane, often with the word ONLY, assigns that lane to the movement shown; a driver in a marked turn-only lane must make that turn, and a through arrow bars turning from that lane. Read the arrows early enough to change lanes lawfully before the intersection.

A stop line is a wide solid white line across the approach lanes that shows where the front of the vehicle must stop; crosswalk lines mark the pedestrian space that must stay clear. Where no stop line exists, the crosswalk edge is the stopping point, and where neither exists, the driver stops where cross traffic first becomes visible.

Chevron and diagonal markings fill painted islands, gore areas and buffer spaces to show pavement that vehicles should not use; drivers stay out of them, do not use them to pass or to jump a queue, and treat a marked gore as the wrong place to change a decision about an exit.

DO NOT BLOCK INTERSECTION markings and signs are used where queues tend to spill back across an intersection; they remind drivers of the rule against stopping in an intersection: enter only when the vehicle can clear the far side.

Texas sets its stopping, standing and parking prohibitions by statute and by official signs: a sign that prohibits stopping or standing must be obeyed, and the state or a local authority may post further restrictions where stopping would be dangerous. There is no statewide curb-color code: the Texas MUTCD directs that parking regulations be established with standard signs, allows a curb marking without words only for the statutory distances from a stop or yield sign, driveway, hydrant or crosswalk, and lets a local agency prescribe its own curb colors to supplement signs.

Except momentarily to pick up or drop off a passenger, a driver may not stand or park in front of a public or private driveway, within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within 30 feet on the approach to a flashing signal, stop sign, yield sign or traffic signal at the side of the road, within 20 feet of a fire station driveway or within 75 feet across the street from a signed fire station entrance, or where an official sign prohibits standing. Stopping is also barred within 30 feet of the ends of a safety zone.

At an intersection with no traffic control device, a driver must stop, yield and grant immediate use of the intersection to a vehicle that has entered from the right or is approaching from the right close enough to be a hazard, and may proceed only when the intersection can be entered safely. Where a device controls the intersection, or a signal is dark, the driver obeys the device or stops as at a stop sign and proceeds only when safe.

At an uncontrolled intersection, a driver on a one-lane or two-lane road meeting a divided highway or a road with three or more marked lanes must stop, yield and grant immediate use of the intersection to traffic on the bigger road; a driver on an unpaved road meeting a paved road must do the same for traffic on the paved road; and a driver on a road that ends at the intersection yields to traffic on the continuing road. In each case the driver proceeds only when the intersection can be entered safely.

Where no traffic signal is operating, a driver must stop and yield to a pedestrian crossing in a crosswalk who is on the driver's half of the roadway or approaching so closely from the other half as to be in danger. A driver coming up behind a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross may not pass it. A pedestrian may not step suddenly off a curb into the path of a vehicle too close to stop.

A pedestrian crossing outside a marked crosswalk or an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection, or where a pedestrian tunnel or bridge is provided, must yield to vehicles on the roadway; between adjacent signalized intersections pedestrians may cross only in a marked crosswalk. An unmarked crosswalk exists at an intersection even without painted lines.

Whatever the right-of-way rule, a driver must exercise due care to avoid hitting a pedestrian on a roadway, sound the horn when necessary as a warning, and take proper precautions on seeing a child or an obviously confused or incapacitated person on the roadway.

A driver approaching an intersection or crosswalk where a pedestrian guided by an assistance animal or carrying a white cane is crossing or trying to cross must take every necessary precaution to avoid injuring or endangering that person, including a full stop when injury or danger can be avoided only by stopping.

YIELD signs control every approach to a roundabout, so entering traffic yields to traffic already circulating; the circulatory roadway itself is never yield-controlled. ONE WAY signs or a roundabout circulation plaque show the counterclockwise direction: enter to the right of the central island, keep moving, and signal the exit. Channelized right-turn lanes behind an island carry their own YIELD sign or signal.

A driver may not turn the vehicle around to travel in the opposite direction when approaching a curve or the crest of a grade if the vehicle cannot be seen by a driver approaching from either direction within 500 feet. Elsewhere a U-turn is lawful unless a sign, signal or local rule prohibits it, and the turning driver yields as for a left turn.

Texas freeways commonly provide a turnaround lane that connects the frontage roads under or beside the overpass so drivers can reverse direction without going through the cross-street intersection; a Turnaround ONLY sign marks the lane and a TURNAROUND guide sign marks its entrance. Using it is the planned way to reverse direction on a frontage road.

A driver may back a vehicle only when the movement can be made safely and without interfering with other traffic, and may never back on the shoulder or roadway of a limited-access or controlled-access highway.
A driver may not begin to move a stopped, standing or parked vehicle unless the movement can be made safely, and must signal before starting from a parked position.

Before leaving a vehicle unattended the driver must stop the engine, lock the ignition, remove the key, set the parking brake effectively, and, when standing on a grade, turn the front wheels to the curb or side of the highway. The engine, ignition and key steps do not apply to a remote-started vehicle that cannot be driven until the key is present.

Parking downhill, turn the front wheels toward the curb; parking uphill beside a curb, turn them away from the curb so the tire rests against it; with no curb, turn them toward the edge of the road in either direction. Set the parking brake and use Park or the proper gear before releasing the pedal.

rules.authoringRule: Outside a business or residence district a driver may not stop, park or leave a vehicle on the main traveled part of a highway unless getting off the roadway is not practicable, a clear width remains for other vehicles, and the vehicle is in clear view for at least 200 feet in each direction. A vehicle disabled where stopping cannot be avoided is excepted.

A driver may not stop, stand or park on the roadway side of a vehicle stopped or parked at the curb (double parking), on a sidewalk, in an intersection, on a crosswalk, between a safety zone and the curb or within 30 feet of the ends of a safety zone, beside a street excavation where it would obstruct traffic, on a bridge or elevated structure or in a tunnel, on a railroad track, or where an official sign prohibits stopping.

On a two-way road a vehicle stops or parks with its right-hand wheels parallel to and within 18 inches of the right curb or edge. On a one-way road it may park parallel to either curb in the direction of traffic, with the wheels on that side within 18 inches of the curb, unless a local ordinance says otherwise. Angle parking is allowed only where a local ordinance permits it.

A person may not open a vehicle door on the side next to moving traffic unless it can be done in reasonable safety without interfering with traffic, and may not leave that door open longer than needed to load or unload a passenger.

Parking spaces marked with the international symbol of access are reserved for vehicles displaying a valid disabled-person placard or license plate, and the striped access aisle beside them must stay clear so a ramp or wheelchair can be used.

rules.authoringRule: On a roadway with two or more marked lanes a driver must stay as nearly as practical within a single lane and may leave it only when the move can be made safely. On a three-lane two-way road the center lane may be used only to pass when it is clear for a safe distance, to prepare for a left turn, or where a device assigns it to your direction. Official devices may assign slow traffic to a lane or prohibit lane changes on a section of road.

A two-way left-turn lane is marked on each side by a solid yellow line with a broken yellow line inside it, often with opposing left-turn arrows; it is reserved for vehicles turning left from either direction and is not a through lane or a passing lane.

On a road wide enough, a driver keeps to the right half of the roadway except when passing, when an obstruction forces a move left after yielding to oncoming traffic, on a three-lane road, or on a one-way road. A driver moving slower than the normal speed of traffic must use the right-hand lane or keep as close as practicable to the right edge unless passing or preparing to turn left. On a two-way road with four or more lanes, no driving left of the center line except as a device or the obstruction rule allows.
On a one-way roadway with three or more lanes, a driver moving into a lane from the right must yield to a vehicle moving into the same lane from the left.

A driver passing on the left must pass at a safe distance and may not return to the right until safely clear of the passed vehicle; when the opposing lane was used, the driver must be back in the proper lane before coming within 200 feet of an approaching vehicle, and otherwise as soon as practicable. Using the left side of the road to pass is allowed only where the law permits it and the left side is clearly visible and free of approaching traffic far enough to complete the pass without interfering with anyone. The driver being passed must move or stay right on an audible signal and may not speed up until completely passed.

A driver may not drive on the left side of the roadway when within 100 feet of an intersection or railroad crossing in a municipality, within 100 feet of one outside a municipality that is marked by a sign or marking, within 100 feet of a bridge, viaduct or tunnel, or while waiting in line for a state ferry. The limits do not apply on a one-way roadway or to a driver turning left into or out of an alley, private road or driveway.
exceptions: left turn into or from an alley, private road or driveway

rules.authoringRule: A driver may pass on the right only when it can be done safely and the vehicle ahead is making or about to make a left turn, and only on a road with unobstructed pavement wide enough for two or more lines of moving vehicles in each direction or on a one-way roadway wide enough for two or more lines. Passing on the right by leaving the main traveled part of the roadway is prohibited except where the improved-shoulder rule allows it.

A driver may drive on a paved (improved) shoulder to the right of the main lanes only when necessary and safe, and only to stop, stand or park; to accelerate before entering the main lane; to slow before a right turn; to pass a vehicle that is slowing or stopped in the main lane, disabled, or preparing to turn left; to let a faster vehicle pass; as a device permits or requires; or to avoid a collision. The left shoulder of a divided or controlled-access highway may be used only to slow or stop a disabled vehicle that cannot safely reach the right shoulder, as a device directs, or to avoid a collision.

Slow vehicle turn-out signs mark paved areas where a slower vehicle can pull aside to let following traffic pass; using one, or the improved shoulder where the law allows it, is how a slow driver releases a queue without stopping in the lane. Re-enter only after signaling and finding a safe gap.

A freeway entrance ramp control signal, or ramp meter, spaces vehicles entering the freeway: stop at the stop line on red, go on green as the signs direct (often one vehicle per green), then use the rest of the ramp to reach freeway speed and merge. A dark ramp meter is simply off, not a stop sign.

HOV, bus, toll and other managed lanes are governed by their own regulatory signs: an occupancy-definition sign says how many people a vehicle needs, an operation sign gives the hours and days, entry and exit are allowed only at the signed openings where the separating line is broken, and priced managed lanes post the toll and payment terms. A solid line or buffer beside the lane means no crossing there.

A bicycle lane is marked with a solid white line, a bicycle symbol and an arrow; it is reserved for bicycles, and a through bicycle lane is placed to the left of a right-turn-only lane. Where a through lane becomes a mandatory right-turn lane, the bicycle lane markings end at least 100 feet before it and a dotted line marks where turning motorists cross; a driver crosses only there, after yielding to any bicyclist in the lane, and a BEGIN RIGHT TURN LANE YIELD TO BIKES sign may confirm the duty.

A flush median island separating opposing traffic is formed by two sets of double solid yellow lines, often filled with yellow diagonal markings; it is not a travel lane, a passing lane or a waiting area, and a driver crosses it only where the law allows a left turn into a driveway or side road. A two-way left-turn lane is marked differently, with a broken yellow line inside a solid one on each side.

A bicyclist has the rights and duties of a vehicle driver. A bicyclist moving slower than traffic rides as near as practicable to the right curb or edge, but may leave the edge to pass, to prepare for a left turn, to avoid a hazard, or when the outside lane is narrower than 14 feet without a bicycle lane or too narrow to share safely; on a one-way road with two or more lanes the bicyclist may ride near the left curb. Bicyclists may ride two abreast in a single lane. Drivers should therefore expect a bicycle to move toward the middle of a narrow lane and give it the lane.

Texas has no statewide minimum passing distance for bicycles in the Transportation Code; a driver must pass at a safe distance and may not return to the lane until safely clear. Many Texas cities set a 3-foot minimum by ordinance, and 3 feet is the practical minimum everywhere: when the lane cannot give that room, change lanes or wait behind the bicyclist.

sources.citation: Texas Driver Handbook (DL-7), revised January 2026 — sharing the road with bicycles
sources.note: Handbook PDF not yet in the dmv-materials library; verify when state-driver-manuals/Texas/DL-7.pdf lands.

rules.reviewNote: Confirm the DL-7 wording on bicycle passing distance and any recommended figure once the PDF lands.

rules.authoringRule: A bicycle must have a brake that can skid the braked wheel on dry pavement, and at night a white front lamp visible from at least 500 feet and a red rear reflector or red lamp visible from 500 feet. Drivers should expect legally lit bicycles after dark and search for them at intersections and driveways.

A motorcyclist is entitled to the full use of a lane, and a motor vehicle may not be driven so as to deprive a motorcycle of it. Two motorcycles may ride abreast in one lane, but a motorcyclist may not ride more than two abreast, may not ride between lanes of traffic moving in the same direction, and may not pass a vehicle while in the same lane as it. Lane splitting is therefore not lawful in Texas.

A slow-moving vehicle must display a reflective slow-moving-vehicle emblem on the rear, visible from at least 500 feet; a golf cart, neighborhood electric vehicle or off-highway vehicle operated at 25 mph or less must display one on a highway. The emblem tells a following driver that the vehicle ahead travels far below traffic speed, so closing distance shrinks quickly.

When an authorized emergency vehicle using its siren and lights, or a police vehicle using either, approaches, a driver must yield, immediately pull parallel to and as close as possible to the right edge or curb clear of any intersection, and stop and stay stopped until it has passed, unless a police officer directs otherwise.

Approaching a stationary emergency vehicle with its lights on, a stationary tow truck with its lights on, a TxDOT or highway maintenance vehicle, a utility service vehicle, a stationary garbage or recycling truck at work, a toll or animal-control vehicle, or a parking-enforcement vehicle using its lights, a driver must, unless a police officer directs otherwise, vacate the lane closest to it when the road has two or more lanes in that direction, or slow to 20 mph below the posted limit (or to 5 mph where the limit is under 25 mph). A violation carries a fine of $500 to $1,250, with higher penalties for repeat offenses or injury.

A driver may not follow within 500 feet of a fire apparatus responding to an alarm or an ambulance flashing red lights, may not drive or park into the block where the fire apparatus has stopped for the alarm, and may not drive over an unprotected fire hose without the commanding fire official's consent.

A driver approaching from either direction a school bus stopped on the highway to load or unload students, with its red flashing lights and stop arm operating, must stop before reaching the bus and may not proceed until the bus moves, the driver signals to proceed, or the signal is turned off. On a highway with separate roadways a driver on the other roadway need not stop, nor on a controlled-access highway where the bus is in a loading zone and pedestrians may not cross. The fine is $500 to $1,250, rising to $1,000 to $2,000 for a repeat offense within five years.
exceptions: school bus on a different roadway of a divided highway
controlled-access highway loading zone where pedestrians may not cross

rules.authoringRule: Light rail transit crossings use crossbucks, STOP or YIELD signs, signals and gates like railroad crossings, and trains in city streets can approach from behind traffic or run beside it. Drivers obey the crossing controls, never turn across the path of an approaching rail vehicle, and stay off the tracks when traffic is stopped ahead.

Approaching a railroad grade crossing, a driver must stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail when a railroad signal warns of a train, a gate is lowered or a flagger warns, a train within about 1,500 feet sounds an audible signal and is an immediate hazard, a train is plainly visible and dangerously close, or a device or signal requires it, and must stay stopped until it is safe and lawful to proceed. At a crossbuck-only crossing the driver yields to any train in hazardous proximity, slows to a reasonable speed, and stops at the stop line or 15 to 50 feet from the rail when safety requires. Driving around, under or through a gate that is closed, closing or opening is an offense.

When a traffic offense is committed in a construction or maintenance work zone while workers are present, and the citation says so, the minimum and maximum fines are doubled; for a prima facie speed limit the doubling applies only if the zone is signed with its maximum lawful speed.

Temporary traffic control in work zones uses orange signs, channelizing cones and drums, barriers, arrow boards, temporary markings and flaggers to move traffic through or around the work. A flagger uses a STOP/SLOW paddle or a red flag, and drivers must follow the flagger and the temporary path in place of the normal lanes.

A vehicle must display its required lights at nighttime, which Texas defines as the period from one-half hour (30 minutes) after sunset to one-half hour (30 minutes) before sunrise, and at any other time when light is insufficient or the weather keeps a person or vehicle from being clearly seen 1,000 feet ahead.

A driver must use a beam that reveals a person or vehicle at a safe distance ahead, but must switch to low beams when approaching an oncoming vehicle within 500 feet and may not use high beams when following another vehicle within 300 feet.

Texas weather signs warn of conditions that recur on a stretch of road: ROAD MAY FLOOD and WATER CROSSING for low places that go under water, WHEN FLOODED TURN AROUND DON'T DROWN with a depth gauge where water crosses the road, GUSTY WINDS AREA where crosswinds move high vehicles, FOG AREA, and WATCH FOR SMOKE ON ROAD. A flooded roadway is never to be entered; depth and current cannot be judged from the driver's seat.

A driver involved in a collision that injures or kills someone, or that damages a vehicle someone is driving or attending, must immediately stop at the scene or as close as possible without obstructing traffic more than necessary, return to the scene if the stop was elsewhere, check whether anyone needs aid, and remain until the information and aid duties are met. On a freeway in a metropolitan area, when every vehicle can still be driven normally and safely, each driver must move the vehicle to a collision investigation site, the frontage road, the nearest suitable cross street or another safe location before exchanging information. Leaving an injury crash is a felony.

At an injury or vehicle-damage crash the driver must give their name and address, the vehicle registration number and the name of their liability insurer to anyone injured and to the driver or occupant of any vehicle involved, show a driver license on request, and give reasonable assistance to anyone injured, including arranging transport to a doctor or hospital when treatment is clearly needed or requested.

A driver who hits an unattended vehicle must stop and either find its driver or owner and give the name and address of the driver and owner of the striking vehicle, or leave a written notice with that information and a statement of the circumstances securely attached in a plainly visible place. A driver who damages only a roadside structure, fixture or landscaping must take reasonable steps to find and notify the owner, giving name, address and registration number and showing a license on request.

When a collision injures or kills a person, or damages a vehicle so that it cannot be driven normally and safely, the driver must immediately notify, by the quickest means, the local police in a municipality, the police or sheriff within 100 feet of a municipality, or otherwise the sheriff or the nearest Department of Public Safety office.

A law enforcement officer who investigates a crash files the written crash report when it caused injury, death, or apparent damage of $1,000 or more to any one person's property. Texas no longer requires a separate driver-filed crash report; the driver's duties are to stop, exchange information, aid the injured and give immediate notice to police when the law requires it.

No one may drive a motor vehicle in Texas unless financial responsibility is established, normally by a liability insurance policy with at least $30,000 for injury or death of one person, $60,000 for two or more persons, and $25,000 for property damage in one collision. On request the driver must show evidence of coverage, on paper or on a phone, to a peace officer or to another driver in a collision. Driving without it is a misdemeanor with a fine of $175 to $350, and $350 to $1,000 for a repeat offense.

A driver may not use a portable wireless communication device to read, write or send an electronic message while operating a motor vehicle unless the vehicle is stopped. It is a defense that the device was used hands-free, for GPS navigation, to report illegal activity or summon emergency help, to enter traffic and road information into an app, or to read a message the driver reasonably believed concerned an emergency.

In a school crossing zone a driver may not use a wireless communication device at all unless the vehicle is stopped or the device is used hands-free; the zone is signed by the local authority. The same hands-free rule applies to a bus driver carrying a minor passenger.

A driver under 18 may not use a wireless communication device while driving, handheld or hands-free, except in an emergency. A driver under 18 also may not drive between midnight and 5 a.m. unless the trip is necessary for work, a school-related activity or a medical emergency, and may not carry more than one passenger under 21 who is not a family member. The night and passenger limits do not apply while a learner-license holder is accompanied as the license requires. A peace officer may not stop a vehicle solely to check for these violations; a phone violation carries a fine of $25 to $99.

Driving a vehicle in wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property is reckless driving, a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $200, up to 30 days in county jail, or both; it applies on highways, other public places and business parking areas.
A vehicle may carry video equipment only if the display is not visible from the driver's seat while the vehicle is out of Park or the parking brake is off.

A person is intoxicated when alcohol, a drug, a controlled substance or any combination takes away the normal use of mental or physical faculties, or when the alcohol concentration is 0.08 or more. Driving while intoxicated in a public place is a Class B misdemeanor with at least 72 hours of confinement; with an open container in the driver's immediate possession the minimum is six days; at 0.15 or more it is a Class A misdemeanor; in a school crossing zone while its reduced limit applies, or with a passenger under 15, it is a state jail felony.

Knowingly possessing an open container of an alcoholic beverage in the passenger area of a motor vehicle on a public highway is an offense whether the vehicle is moving, stopped or parked. The passenger area does not include a locked glove compartment or similar locked storage, the trunk, or the area behind the last upright seat in a vehicle without a trunk; passengers in a bus, taxi, limousine or the living quarters of a motor home are excepted.
exceptions: area behind the last upright seat when there is no trunk
passengers in a bus, taxi, limousine or motor-home living quarters

rules.authoringRule: A minor, a person under 21, commits an offense by operating a motor vehicle in a public place with any detectable amount of alcohol in the system; a first offense is a Class C misdemeanor and the court orders 20 to 40 hours of alcohol-related community service, with license suspension consequences under the driver license laws.

A person arrested for driving while intoxicated, or for a minor's alcohol offense, is deemed to have consented to giving breath or blood specimens for alcohol or drug analysis. Refusing a peace officer's request brings a license suspension of 180 days, or two years when the driving record shows an alcohol- or drug-related enforcement contact in the previous 10 years, separate from any criminal case.

When a specimen shows a prohibited alcohol concentration, or a minor tests positive, the driver license is suspended administratively: 90 days for an adult with no alcohol- or drug-related enforcement contact in the previous 10 years and one year with a prior contact; for a minor, 60 days for a first offense, 120 days for a second and 180 days for a third.

Everyone at least 15 years old riding in a passenger vehicle must be secured by a safety belt in any seat that has one, front or back. The driver commits an offense by allowing a child under 17 who is not required to be in a child safety seat to ride unbelted in a seat that has a belt.

A child younger than 8 must ride secured in a child passenger safety seat system used according to the manufacturer's instructions unless the child is taller than 4 feet 9 inches; the fine is $25 to $250. Texas law sets no separate rear-facing age, so the seat's own instructions decide when a child moves from rear-facing to forward-facing and then to a booster. Vehicles for hire and vehicles in which every belted seat is already occupied are excepted.
rules.reviewNote: The DL-7 may recommend rear-facing until age 2 as guidance; confirm before adding any rear-facing age.

rules.authoringRule: A driver may not operate an open-bed pickup or flatbed truck, or tow an open flatbed trailer, with a child under 18 riding in the bed; the fine is $25 to $200, with defenses for parades, emergencies, farm work on rural roads, beaches, a household's only vehicle and permitted hayrides.

Leaving a young child alone in a vehicle is an offense in Texas and a heat emergency in minutes; a parked car heats far faster than the air outside. Never leave a child or a dependent adult alone in a vehicle, and check the whole vehicle before locking it.

sources.citation: Texas Driver Handbook (DL-7), revised January 2026 — leaving children unattended in vehicles
sources.note: Handbook PDF not yet in the dmv-materials library; verify when state-driver-manuals/Texas/DL-7.pdf lands.

rules.reviewNote: Penal Code § 22.10 (child under 7, longer than 5 minutes, no one 14 or older present) is not in the dmv-materials library; add the snapshot before teaching the exact ages.

rules.authoringRule: A motor vehicle must have a horn in good working order audible from at least 200 feet, used only when necessary for safe operation; a mirror giving the driver a view of the highway at least 200 feet behind; a working windshield wiper; a muffler that prevents excessive noise; working brakes; and the required lamps and reflectors.

A driver may not drive a vehicle loaded, or with more than three people in the front seat, so that the view to the front or sides is obstructed or the driver's control of the vehicle is interfered with, and a passenger may not ride in a position that does either.

A load that extends 4 feet or more beyond the rear of the vehicle must carry two red lamps visible from 500 feet, red reflectors and side red lamps at night, and at other times red flags at least 12 inches square marking its extremities; a load wider than the vehicle is flagged the same way.

Texas no longer requires an annual safety inspection for non-commercial vehicles; owners pay an inspection replacement fee at registration, and vehicles in the listed emissions counties (including Harris, Dallas, Tarrant, Travis, Bexar-area and other metropolitan counties named by TxDMV) must pass an emissions inspection before registration. Commercial vehicles still need a safety inspection. The driver is therefore responsible for keeping brakes, tires, lights, horn, mirrors and wipers in working order.

sources.citation: Texas Department of Motor Vehicles — New to Texas

rules.authoringRule: A learner license may be issued to a person at least 15 and under 18 who has completed and passed the classroom phase of an approved driver education course, meets the school-attendance requirement, and has passed every part of the license examination except the driving test. The holder may drive only with the license in possession and a licensed driver who is at least 21 and has at least one year of driving experience seated beside the operator.

A driver under 18 may receive a Class C license only if at least 16, holding a certificate of a completed approved driver education course, meeting the school-attendance rule (a diploma, at least 80 days of attendance in the preceding semester, or 45 days of enrollment in an equivalency program), providing written parental permission for school-record checks, passing the examination, and having held a learner license for at least six months. The under-18 phone, night and passenger restrictions then continue until the driver turns 18.

No one under 25 receives a Texas driver license without a certificate showing completion of an approved driver education course; an applicant who is 18 or older may take the shorter adult driver education course. A person who holds a valid license from another state is exempt.

The license examination tests vision; the ability to identify and understand English highway signs that regulate, warn or direct; knowledge of Texas traffic laws; knowledge of motorists' rights and responsibilities toward bicyclists; knowledge of how wireless devices and other distractions affect safe driving; and a demonstration of ordinary and reasonable vehicle control. The applicant may take the knowledge parts in writing, and a licensed driver education provider may administer the vision, sign and traffic-law parts to its students. The examination is held within 10 days of application.

The Texas Driver Handbook describes the knowledge test as passed at 70 percent, and requires applicants to complete the free Impact Texas Drivers (ITD) video course before taking the driving test. Vision screening is part of every application.

sources.citation: Texas Driver Handbook (DL-7), revised January 2026 — knowledge test and Impact Texas Drivers

rules.authoringRule: No one may drive on a Texas highway without a driver license unless expressly exempt. The driver must carry the license of the appropriate class while driving and display it on demand of a magistrate, court officer or peace officer; a peace officer may stop a driver to check for it, and a first violation carries a fine of up to $200.

A new Texas resident who is at least 16 and carries a valid license from the previous state or country may drive on it for no more than 90 days after entering the state, and must obtain a Texas license within that time.
A license holder who moves to a new residence address, or changes their name, must notify the Department of Public Safety within 30 days and apply for a duplicate license showing the current address.
Within 30 days of buying a vehicle or becoming a Texas resident, the owner must apply to register it through the county tax assessor-collector for each year it is used on a public highway.

The buyer of a used vehicle must file the assigned title with the county tax assessor-collector within 30 days of the assignment date, which also applies for transfer of registration; active-duty military members have 60 days. The seller protects themselves by submitting a vehicle transfer notification to the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles, on paper or online, giving the vehicle description, both parties' names and the date possession was delivered.

The Department of Public Safety suspends a license when the driver drove while the license was suspended or revoked, is a habitually reckless or negligent operator, is a habitual violator (four or more moving-violation convictions from separate incidents in 12 consecutive months, or seven or more in 24 months), was responsible as a driver for a collision causing serious injury or serious property damage, is under 18 with two or more moving violations in a 12-month period, or fled from a police officer.

Texas no longer assigns points to a driving record; the Driver Responsibility Program that did so was repealed, and license actions now follow conviction counts and specific offenses under the Transportation Code rather than a point total.

rules.authoringRule: After a conviction for driving while intoxicated and related offenses, when the license is suspended, the judge must generally restrict the driver to a vehicle fitted with an ignition interlock device — a breath tester wired to the starter — at the driver's own expense, for the period of the suspension, unless the court waives it for good cause.

Wilfully failing to stop, or fleeing or trying to elude a pursuing police vehicle after a hand, voice, light or siren signal from a uniformed officer in a marked vehicle, is a Class B misdemeanor; it becomes a Class A misdemeanor when the driver recklessly puts someone in danger of serious injury, and it is also a ground for license suspension.

A driver who was under 21 at the time of the offense loses the license automatically on conviction of driving while intoxicated or of an alcohol, drug or volatile-chemical offense; a DWI-type conviction brings a one-year suspension regardless of any education program.
